headline: Who Is Rohit Prasad? The Ranchi Engineer Who Built Alexa — and Now Runs Boston Dynamics
subheadline: The speech scientist who put a voice assistant in hundreds of millions of homes left Amazon at the end of 2025. On October 7 he became only the third CEO in Boston Dynamics' 34 years — hired to give the world's most famous robots a brain.
body:
• Rohit Prasad, the Ranchi-born engineer who built Amazon's Alexa into a service used in hundreds of millions of households, became CEO of Boston Dynamics on October 7, 2026.
  • He is only the third chief executive in the robotics company's 34-year history, and the first hired specifically to fuse AI with machines that move.
  • His career runs in one line: speech coding in Chicago, 14 years of language research at Raytheon BBN, 12 years at Amazon, and the Amazon Nova foundation models.
  • For the diaspora, his rise is the pattern at its highest level: an engineer from Jharkhand now deciding how humanoid robots enter factories — starting with Hyundai's Georgia plant in 2028.

The most famous robot company in the world is now run by a speech scientist from Ranchi. On October 7, 2026, Rohit Prasad took over as chief executive of Boston Dynamics, the Hyundai-owned maker of the Spot quadruped, the Stretch warehouse robot and the Atlas humanoid. He succeeds a line of mechanical engineers. What Hyundai bought with this hire is different: the man who taught machines to listen, now in charge of teaching them to move.

Prasad arrived at Boston Dynamics after 12 years at Amazon, where he served as senior vice president and head scientist for Alexa and artificial general intelligence, and before that nearly 14 years at Raytheon BBN Technologies. According to Reuters, the appointment positions him to turn the company's physical AI breakthroughs into commercial products — the same trick he pulled off with Alexa, which grew from a skunkworks project into a service used in hundreds of millions of households.

"Boston Dynamics is uniquely positioned to advance Physical AI through its world-class robotics expertise. I am honored to join the company at such a pivotal moment for the industry."

— Rohit Prasad, CEO, Boston Dynamics

Ranchi to Chicago: a speech scientist is formed

Prasad grew up in Ranchi, in what is now Jharkhand, and schooled at DAV in the city. In 1997 he graduated in electronics and communication engineering from the Birla Institute of Technology, Mesra — choosing, by his own later account, to study close to home despite other offers. His family still lives in Ranchi, and he has said he returns roughly every year and a half.

https://x.com/arnaudmercier/status/2111423142493122845

The move to the United States took him to the Illinois Institute of Technology in Chicago, where he completed a master's degree in electrical engineering in 1999. His research there — low-bit-rate speech coding for wireless applications — sounds narrow. It was, in hindsight, the foundation of everything that followed: how to squeeze human speech into signals a machine can work with.

Fourteen years at BBN

In 1999 Prasad joined BBN Technologies in Cambridge, Massachusetts — the research firm that built ARPANET, the internet's ancestor, and one of the world's leading centres for speech and language research. He stayed nearly 14 years, rising from staff scientist to deputy manager and senior director of its Speech, Language and Multimedia business unit after BBN became part of Raytheon.

The work was unglamorous and deep: speech recognition, speech-to-speech translation, natural language processing and machine learning, built for US government and commercial clients. It made Prasad something rare in consumer technology — an executive whose understanding of language machines came from research benches, not product decks.

Building Alexa

Amazon hired him in 2013 as director of machine learning for a secretive project inside its Lab126 hardware division: a computer you could talk to. The first Echo speaker shipped in 2014. Prasad later described the assignment as a Star Trek idea that bordered on impossible — a machine that could hear a command across a noisy room, understand it, and act.

He rose with the product: vice president and head scientist of Alexa AI, then, in 2021, senior vice president and head scientist for Alexa overall. By 2023, customers had bought well over half a billion Alexa-enabled devices. In 2017, Fast Company ranked him ninth on its list of the 100 most creative people in business, and Recode put him on its list of the 100 people who mattered most in technology, business and media.

The Nova years — and a December exit

In mid-2023, Prasad moved up again: senior vice president and head scientist for artificial general intelligence, reporting directly to CEO Andy Jassy, with Amazon racing to answer ChatGPT. His organisation built the Amazon Nova family of foundation models, launched at the end of 2024 and used by enterprises through Amazon Bedrock. TIME named him to its TIME100 AI list of the most influential people in artificial intelligence in 2024.

His exit was not a coronation lap. In December 2025, Jassy announced that Prasad would leave at the end of the year, folding the model teams into a new organisation under cloud veteran Peter DeSantis that also covers custom silicon and quantum computing. The reshuffle came as Amazon worked to close ground on OpenAI and Google, and as Alexa's long-delayed generative-AI rebuild drew scrutiny. Prasad left with the platform he built in hundreds of millions of homes — and with the harder, model-era chapter of Amazon's AI story still being argued over.

Why a robot company wanted a voice man

Boston Dynamics, founded in 1992 as an MIT spinout, has had only two chief executives before him: founder Marc Raibert, who ran it until 2020, and Robert Playter, who stepped down in February 2026 after six years; finance chief Amanda McMaster served as interim CEO. Playter's departure was followed by other senior exits, including chief technology officer Aaron Saunders. Prasad is also expected to join the board, subject to approval.

Hyundai Motor Group, which took majority control in 2021 and is now moving to buy out SoftBank's remaining stake, has put dates on the ambition. It plans to deploy Atlas humanoids at its Georgia plant from 2028, build capacity to produce 30,000 robots a year, and has partnerships with Nvidia and Google DeepMind to develop the humanoid. The robots are expected to start with tasks like parts sequencing, welding and logistics before moving to component assembly by 2030. Spot already inspects industrial sites and Stretch already unloads trailers — revenue today, while Atlas is the bet on tomorrow.

"Boston Dynamics' industry-leading robotics, Rohit's proven ability to turn AI into products at global scale, and Hyundai Motor Group's modern manufacturing, logistics, and mobility capabilities give us a powerful foundation to build and scale Physical AI."

— Jaehoon Chang, Vice Chair, Hyundai Motor Group

What to watch

Prasad's task is the one that has defeated every robotics company before him: turning astonishing demonstrations into dependable, affordable machines that factories actually buy in volume. His record argues both ways. Alexa proved he can scale a new interface to half a billion devices; the Nova era showed how hard it is to catch leaders who moved first. Boston Dynamics gives him something Amazon never did — the world's best robot bodies, a parent with factories of its own to deploy them in, and a 2028 deadline that is already on the calendar.

For Indian engineers watching from Ranchi, Bengaluru or New Jersey, the arc is the story: a boy who chose the engineering college near home, spent 26 years in one American metro area, and now runs the company whose dancing robots the whole internet has seen. The next era of AI, his appointment says, will not just talk. It will walk — and an Indian-born scientist is in charge of teaching it how.
